...can we love children and health if we do not have them, even if we desire them? This makes me hold that love and desire are two contrary affections of the **will**, and you have told me that both can exist together; clarify this doubt for me.

**PHI.** If love is only for things that have **being** <note>Italian: *essere*. In this philosophical context, "being" refers to actual existence or presence as opposed to potentiality or absence.</note>, why would desire not also be for those same things?

**SO.** Because just as love presupposes the being of things, so desire presupposes their **privation** <note>Italian: *priuatione*. A technical term in Aristotelian philosophy meaning the absence or lack of a quality or thing that should naturally be there.</note>.

**PHI.** For what reason does love presuppose the being of things?

**SO.** Because **knowledge** must precede love, for nothing could be loved if it were not first known under the **guise of good** <note>Italian: *spetie di buona*. This refers to the concept *sub specie boni*—the idea that the human will only moves toward things that the intellect perceives as being "good" in some way.</note>; and nothing falls within our knowledge unless it is first actually found in being, because our mind is a mirror and example—or better said, an image—of real things, so that there is nothing that can be loved unless it is first found to really exist.

**PHI.** You speak the truth; but for this very same reason, desire cannot apply except to things that have being, because we do not desire anything except those things that we first know under the guise of good. And for this reason, **the Philosopher** <note>A common title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance. This refers to the opening of his *Nicomachean Ethics*: "The good is that which all things desire."</note> defined the **good** as that which everyone desires, since knowledge is of things that have being.

**SO.** It cannot be denied that knowledge precedes desire; but rather, I would say that not only is every **cognition** <note>Italian: *cognitione*. The process of acquiring knowledge or the knowledge itself.</note> of things that are, but also of those that are not, because our **intellect**...

**PHI.** Knowledge of the loved or desired thing as being **good** <note>The "guise of good" (sub specie boni) is a central theme here: the idea that the will only pursues what the mind perceives as beneficial or beautiful, even if that perception is mistaken.</note> precedes both love and desire. **SO.** If desire presupposed the being of things, it would follow that whenever we judge a thing to be good and desirable, such a judgment would always be true; but do you not see that many times it is false, and the thing is not found to be so in its being? **PHI.** This very same defect you mention happens no less in love than in desire; for many times that thing which is esteemed good and lovable is actually bad <note>Italian: *gattiua* (modern *cattiva*).</note> and ought to be abhorred. And just as the **truth** of the judgment of things causes right and virtuous desires—from which derive all virtues, temperate acts, and praiseworthy works—so the **falsehood** of such judgment is the cause of bad desires and dishonest loves, from which all human vices and errors derive. ...in the **being** <note>Italian: *essere*. In this philosophical context, Philo argues that for something to be thought of, it must have some form of existence, even if only in the mind.</note> of the thing. 

**SO.** I cannot fly so high with you, O Philo; let us come, I pray you, a bit lower. I still see that none of those things we most desire are properly loved. 

**PHI.** We certainly always desire that which we do not have, but not for that reason that which **is not**; on the contrary, **desire** usually concerns things that exist, but which we are unable to possess. 

**SO.** Yet it also usually concerns those things that do not actually exist, and we desire that they *should* exist, though we do not necessarily desire to "possess" them. For example, we desire that it should rain when it is not raining, and that there be good weather, and that a friend should arrive, and that something should be done. Because these things **are not** <note>Italian: *non sonno*. Thus, desire is of things that are not. 

**PHI.** That which has no being at all is nothing; and that which is nothing, just as it cannot be loved, so too can it be neither desired nor possessed. And these things you mentioned—even if they do not have a present, actual existence when they are desired—nevertheless, their being is **possible**. One can desire that a **possible being** <note>Italian: *essere possibile*. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo concerning the nature of desire and existence. The previous page ended with Philo beginning to explain that one can desire things that do not yet exist because their "being" is potential. This page picks up that thought, arguing that for something to be desired, it must first possess the attributes of being, truth, and goodness.</meta>

...rather because they are founded in the **being** <note>Italian: *essere*. Philo uses this term to denote existence or the essential nature of a thing.</note> of the thing, and not in its non-being; and for a thing to be desirable, three titles must precede it in order. The first is **being**; the second, **truth**; and third, that it be **good**. And with these attributes, it comes to be loved and desired, which could not happen if it were not first estimated as good—for in no other way would it be loved or desired. And before it is judged good, it must be known as true; and as it is actually found in existence before it is known, it must have real **being**, because the thing first exists in its being, then it is imprinted upon the **intellect**, then it is judged to be good, and ultimately it is loved and desired. For this reason, the **Philosopher** <note>A standard reference to Aristotle, the cornerstone of medieval and Renaissance philosophy.</note> says that being, truth, and goodness are convertible into one <note>Philosophical original: *ens, verum, et bonum convertuntur*. This means that everything that truly exists is also "true" in its nature and "good" in its purpose.</note>—except that being is in itself; truth is when it is impressed upon the intellect; and goodness is when it moves from the intellect and the will toward the acquisition of things through love and desire. Thus, desire presupposes being no less than love does.

**SO.** I still see that we desire many things whose being is not only lacking in the one who desires them, but even in the things themselves—such as health and children when we do not have them—in which cases certainly love does not apply, but only desire.

**PHI.** That which is desired—even if it is lacking to the one desiring it and has no proper being in itself—is not, for all that, entirely deprived of being (as you say). Rather, it must in some way have being; otherwise, it could not be known as good or desired. Even if it does not have its own proper being—and thus I say of health in a sick person, who desires...

<meta>This page transitions from the philosophical dialogue between Sophia and Philo to the book's formal dedication. While the previous discussion explored the nature of desire and being, this section is an introductory address by Mariano Lenzi to his patron, Aurelia Petrucci, framing her as a living embodiment of the wisdom discussed in the text.</meta>

# MARIANO LENZI
## TO THE VALIANT LADY AURELIA PETRUCCI. <note>The Italian *Valorosa Madonna* implies not just courage, but a noble excellence and intellectual strength highly praised in Renaissance women of status.</note>

It was a most ancient custom of the writers of Egypt to address the most holy books written by them to Mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*. Here referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary syncretic figure of the Egyptian god Thoth and the Greek Hermes, credited with the invention of writing and science.</note>, because they estimated that all the arts, all the sciences, and all beautiful things had been discovered by Mercury, and that to him, as the inventor of every thing, it was fitting to render thanks for whatever man learned or knew. And for this reason Pythagoras, and Plato, and many other great philosophers went to Egypt to learn philosophy, and for the most part they learned it from the columns of Mercury, which were all full of wisdom and of doctrine. 

I likewise, Valiant Lady, judge that whatever can be done by those who have known the highness of your soul is fitting for you, and that their beautiful thoughts, nourished by your divine spirit, should return to you, and strive as much as they can in honor of your name. For they learn true virtues <note>original: *uirtù*. This term encompasses moral excellence, intellectual power, and the classical concept of "virtù" or effective character.</note> no less from the example of your life than those ancient philosophers did from the columns of Mercury. For if one considers the nobility, the highness, and the refinement of your soul; if one regards how much honesty, courtesy, and grace are present; if one considers what prudence, discernment, and wisdom are there; and finally, if every one of your virtues is gazed upon part by part, it is certainly seen by refined minds <note>original: *gl'ingegni purgati*. Literally "purged wits," referring to those whose intellects are cleared of common prejudices and are capable of perceiving higher truths.</note> that your life is nothing other than a mirror, and an Ideal <note>original: *Idea*. Used in the Platonic sense of a perfect, divine archetype or pattern.</note> of the way in which it is fitting for others to live. And those who, mired in earthly things...

<summary>In this dedication, Mariano Lenzi compares the noblewoman Aurelia Petrucci to the legendary Pillars of Mercury, suggesting her life serves as a perfect instructional "mirror" of virtue and wisdom for others to follow, just as ancient philosophers studied in Egypt.</summary>
<keywords>Mariano Lenzi, Aurelia Petrucci, dedication, Mercury, Hermes Trismegistus, Egypt, Pythagoras, Plato, virtue, Renaissance humanism, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues Mariano Lenzi's dedication to Aurelia Petrucci, transitioning from the comparison of her virtue to the columns of Mercury to the editor's justification for publishing Leone Ebreo's work under her patronage.</meta>

cannot rise in an instant to this heavenly thought, yet as long as they turn their eyes toward you—illuminated by your ray—they are gradually purified, and make themselves worthy of the high <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: *contemplatione*. In a Neoplatonic sense, this refers to the soul's intellectual ascent toward divine truth.</note> of your divinity. Recognizing therefore this debt, both common to all and my own, I have done as those do who, unable to satisfy a debt from their own resources, pay with those of others. Desiring to discharge part of this great obligation that I have toward you, and because of the poverty of my own intellect, being unable to send you fruit grown in my own garden, I send it to you grown in the gardens of others.

That is to say, the books of love by <term>Master Leone</term> <note>original: *Maestro Leone*. Referring to Leone Ebreo (Judah Leon Abravanel), a Jewish philosopher whose *Dialogues of Love* (c. 1502) explored the intersection of Platonic philosophy and Jewish mysticism.</note> under the title of <term>Philo</term> and <term>Sophia</term> <note>original: *Philone & Sophia*. The interlocutors of the dialogues; their names literally mean "Lover" and "Wisdom" in Greek.</note>: a chaste subject of love for a chaste lady who inspires love; heavenly thoughts for a Lady who is adorned with heavenly virtue; the highest understandings for a lady full of the highest concepts. Thus I have wished, rather than prolonging the satisfaction of such a debt due to my own poverty, to show you with the work of another the soul I have to satisfy you.

Though I estimate (whenever I think of it) that I make two no small gains at once: to release part of this obligation to you, and to place under obligation to me—if shadows can be so bound—<term>Master Leone</term>. For since I have drawn these divine dialogues of his out of the darkness in which they lay buried, and placed them as if in clear light, and recommended them to the name of so valiant a lady as you are, I believe for certain that he must rejoice exceedingly. He must remain much obligated to me for this, his new splendor and for such high protection. You, therefore, having become as it were the guardian of this work, by directing your ray upon it—as upon a body most fit to receive light—will make it appear more splendid and more miraculous to the world.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia regarding the philosophical definitions of love and desire. Philo is clarifying his previous statement about the necessity of "being" (existence) for a thing to be truly loved rather than merely desired.</meta>

...they say they are loved because they are esteemed as good, but speaking correctly, those things that have no <term>being</term> <note>original: *essere proprio*. In this metaphysical context, "being" refers to the actual, individual existence of a thing.</note> of their own cannot be called loved, such as health and children when we lack them. I speak of **real love**, for **imagined [love]** can be had for all desired things, because of the "being" they possess in the imagination. From this imagined being, a certain love is born, the subject of which is not the actual real thing desired—since it does not yet have being in reality—but only the concept of that thing taken from its general existence. Of such love, the subject is improper because it is not true love, as it lacks a real subject; it is only simulated and imagined, because the desire for such things is stripped of true love.

So it is that among things, three kinds of love and desire are found:

1.  Some are **loved and desired together**, such as truth, wisdom, and a worthy person when we do not possess them.
2.  Others are **loved and not desired**, such as all good things already had and possessed.
3.  Some others are **desired and not loved**, such as health and children when we lack them, and other things that have no real being.

Therefore, the things loved and desired together are those that are esteemed as good, have their own being, and which we lack. The loved and not desired are those same things when we have and possess them. And the things desired and not loved are those that not only do we lack, but which also do not have being in themselves, in which [love] could fall... <note>The text ends mid-sentence on the word "ca-" (likely *cadere*, meaning "to fall" or "to take hold").</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is explaining that while desire and love often overlap, a thing must have its own "real being" (existence) to be truly loved. ...to place love. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought from the previous page: "...in which [one could] place love."</note>

**SOPHIA.** I have heard your discourse, which pleases me greatly; but I see many things that have their own real being, and when we do not have them, we desire them, but we do not love them until they are obtained. At that point they are loved and no longer desired—such as wealth, a house, a vineyard, or a jewel. While these are in the power of others, they are desired and not loved because they belong to another; but once they are acquired, and the desire for them ceases, love is placed in them. Thus, before they are acquired, they are only desired and not loved, and after they are acquired, they are only loved and not desired.

**PHILO.** In this, you have spoken the truth. I do not say that all desired things (which have their own being) are also loved; rather, I have affirmed that those which are desired must likewise have their own being <note>original: *essere proprio*. Philo distinguishes between things that exist in reality versus those that exist only in the imagination.</note>, because otherwise, even if they are desired, they cannot be loved. For this reason, I did not give you the example of a jewel or a house, but of virtue, wisdom, or a worthy person; for these, when they are lacking, are likewise loved and desired.

**SOPHIA.** Tell me the cause of this difference found among desired things that have their own being: why can some of those be loved while they are desired, and some cannot?

**PHILO.** The cause and the difference lie in the nature of lovable things, which (as you know) are of three kinds: **Useful, Delectable, and Honorable** <note>original: *Utili, Delettabili, &amp; honeſte*. **SOPHIA.** Declare to me the difference between them—that is, between loving and desiring—and so that I may better understand you, I would like you to provide a definition.

<meta>This page continues Philo’s explanation of the nature of love and desire. Having previously discussed "useful things" (wealth and utility), he now examines "delightful things" (sensory pleasures), explaining how love and desire for them are fleeting compared to more intellectual or moral pursuits.</meta>

[de]lightful things <note>The word begins from the previous page's catchword "delettabili."</note> have this property: that once they are possessed, just as the desire for them ceases, so too, most of the time, does the love for them; and many times it turns into disgust and loathing. This is because one who is hungry or thirsty, after he is satiated, no longer desires to eat or drink; rather, it becomes offensive to him. The same occurs in other things that provide material delight, because with a tiresome <term>satiety</term> <note>The state of being fed or gratified beyond capacity, leading to boredom or disgust.</note>, the desire for them likewise ceases, so that in delightful things, both love and desire live and die together. It is true, however, that among delightful things one finds some <term>intemperate</term> <note>People who lack self-control and indulge in pleasures to excess.</note> people—just as they are found among the "useful" things—who are never satisfied, nor do they ever seek to be satisfied. Such are the gluttons, the drunkards, and the lecherous, who dislike satiety and quickly return anew to the desire and love of those things, or rather to the desire of others of that same kind.

The desire for such delightful things is properly called <term>appetite</term>, just as the desire for useful things is called <term>ambition</term> or <term>cupidity</term> <note>An eager or excessive desire, especially for money or possessions.</note>. The excess of desiring these things which give specific delight, and the dwelling in them, is called <term>luxury</term> <note>original: "lussuria"; in this context, it refers to excessive indulgence in any sensory pleasure, not just sexual lust.</note>, which may be true carnal lust, or gluttony, or other superfluous delicacies, or undue softness. Those who nourish themselves in such vices are called <term>lechers</term>; and when reason resists the vice in some part, even if it is overcome by it, then such vicious people are called <term>incontinent</term> <note>From the Greek "akrasia": knowing what is right but lacking the will to do it.</note>. But those who abandon reason entirely, without seeking to resist the vicious habit in any part, are called <term>intemperate</term> <note>original: "distemparati"; those who have lost the ability to even recognize what is right, having been entirely corrupted by habit.</note>. And just as this extreme of luxury is found in de[lightful things...]

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia, moving from the definition of "luxury" to the ethical "middle way" regarding sensory pleasures. Philo contrasts the excess of indulgence with the excess of abstinence, ultimately defining the virtues of temperance and fortitude.</meta>

[delec]table <note>The word completes "delettabili" from the previous page; the catchword "ni" in the metadata may refer to a variant spelling or a transition from a word like "beni" (goods).</note> things, a vice corresponding to avarice and cupidity in the realm of the useful; likewise, I consider the other extreme of superfluous <term>abstinence</term> to be a vice, which in the useful realm corresponds to the vice of <term>prodigality</term> <note>Wasteful extravagance; here Philo argues that denying oneself necessary pleasure is as much a deviation from reason as wasting money.</note>. This is because the former is an attachment to material goods <note>original: "una á la robba"</note> that is not suitable for an honorable life, and the latter abandons the pleasure necessary for the sustenance of life and the preservation of health.

The middle ground between these two extremes is a very great virtue and is called <term>continence</term>. When reason, through virtue, conquers the still-persistent stimulation of our physical senses, it is called <term>temperance</term>—this is when sensuality completely ceases to provoke the virtuous reason. Both consist in restraining oneself temperately regarding delightful things, without lacking what is necessary and without taking what is superfluous.

Some call this virtue <term>fortitude</term> <note>original: "forteza"; usually meaning physical strength, but here used for moral "strength of soul."</note> and they say that the truly strong man is he who conquers himself. This is because delightful things have more power over <term>human nature</term> than useful things do, as pleasure is the means by which nature preserves its own being. Therefore, he who can moderate this excess can, in truth, be called the conqueror of his most powerful and internal enemy.

**PHILO.** It incites the <term>appetite</term> <note>original: "appetito"; here referring to the natural or sensory drive for something one perceives as good.</note> no less, and sharpens the desire and taste for them, just as it enlivens love; and you know that nothing is craved or desired except that which is lacking.

**SOPHIA.** Now how does this work? For we see that delightful things, once possessed, are not only loved but still craved; therefore, that which one has must [somehow] be lacking and not possessed.

For once they are had, their company arrives, and the appetite and the love for them are equally lost; because while they are being acquired, the lack does not cease until <term>satiety</term> <note>A state of complete fullness or satisfaction where the desire for more vanishes.</note> is reached. In fact, I say that with the first taste, one’s knowledge is strained by the closeness of the delightful thing, and with this, the appetite is further incited and love is enlivened. The cause is the feeling of <term>privation</term> <note>original: "priuatione"; the state of being deprived of something, or the absence of a quality.</note>, which, through the presence and partial participation in the taste of the delightful thing that is lacking, becomes stronger and more stinging. And when one tastes so much of such delights that they reach satiety, it entirely removes the lack; and with that, the appetite and love for such delight simultaneously cease and turn into disgust and dislike. Thus, appetite and love are joined to the lack of the delightful thing, and not to the possession of it.

**SOPHIA.** What you have said is enough for me on this point. But having stated in what ways the <term>useful</term> <note>original: "utile"; things valued for their function or gain rather than immediate sensory pleasure.</note> and the delightful are similar and different in the logic of loving and desiring—following the cause of their manifest similarity—the reason for the diversity or opposition of the <term>will</term> <note>original: "uolontá"; the intellectual or conscious faculty of choice, distinguished here from mere sensory appetite.</note> remains hidden to me...

**PHILO.** The cause is the difference in how these two kinds of loved and desired things are enjoyed. Because the useful consists in the continuous possession of the thing, the more it is possessed, the more its utility is enjoyed; for this reason, love does not arrive until it is possessed and desire ceases, and then it continues while it is possessed. And if possession is lacking—or truly ceases after it has been had—although there may be desire, there will not, however, be love. 

But regarding the delightful, its pleasure does not consist in possession, nor in <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habito"; here meaning a settled disposition or the stable state of having something.</note>, nor in perfect acquisition, but in a certain attention mixed with <term>lack</term> <note>original: "mancamento"; the state of wanting or missing something even while experiencing it.</note>; which, once it ceases entirely, causes the pleasure to vanish, and consequently the appetite and the love for such a delightful thing also cease.

**SOPHIA.** It seems reasonable to me that desire requires the lack of the delightful thing; but it would seem to me that love rather requires the present enjoyment of the delightful. Thus, love for the delightful should exist only insofar as it delights, and not before when it is lacking, nor afterward when it <term>satiates</term> <note>original: "fatia"; to be full to the point of no longer desiring.</note>.

For this reason, the satisfaction they bring is not tedious; and even more so because they are not desired only through pure sensual appetite, but also through the **will** directed by the **rational mind**, which is the unerring governor of nature. For (as **the Philosopher** <note>A standard reference to Aristotle, likely referring here to his *Economics* or *De Anima*, where he discusses procreation as a means for mortals to participate in the eternal.</note> says), since animals lack individual perpetuity and know themselves to be mortal, they desire to be immortal at least through their children. This is the desire for the only possible **immortality** for mortal creatures. Because the delight of children differs in this way from other delightful things, it follows that once they are had, they do not lead to a tedious satiety. In this, they are similar to health, which not only through its possession [con...] <meta>catchword: cef, likely for "conferma" (confirms) or "continua" (continues).</meta>

It is indeed true that, although honor is the reward of **virtue** <term>uirtù: moral excellence and strength of character</term>, it is not, however, the proper goal of honorable and virtuous acts, nor should one act for the sake of it. These are indeed the rewards that the virtuous should duly achieve, but not the goal that moves them to perform illustrious works. One should praise honest virtue, but one should not practice virtue in order to be praised; and even though those who offer praise cause virtue to grow, it would rather diminish if that praise were the very goal for which the act was done. However, because of the connection that such delights have with the honorable, they are always appreciated and loved, and one always desires to increase them.

...to know from you about human friendship and divine love—of what strength they are and of what nature. 

PHI. Human friendship is sometimes for **utility** <term>l'utile: material benefit or profit</term> and sometimes for **pleasure** <term>il delettabile: that which provides enjoyment or delight</term>. However, these do not make for perfect friends, nor is it a firm friendship; for once the occasion for such friendships is removed—by which I mean, when the utility and the pleasure cease—the friendships born from them end and dissolve. 

But true human friendship is that which is the cause of **integrity** <term>l'honesto: moral nobility or that which is good for its own sake</term> and the bond of **virtue** <term>uirtù: moral excellence</term>. Such a bond is indissoluble and generates a firm and entirely perfect friendship. Among all human friendships, this alone is the most commended and praised. It serves to bind friends together in such great humanity that the good or ill belonging to each of them is common to both. Sometimes the good delights, and the ill grieves, the friend more than the person actually experiencing them. 

Often, a man takes on a portion of his friend's troubles to lighten them, or truly to assist him through friendship in his labors; for companionship in tribulations causes them to be felt less. The **philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, who discusses friendship extensively in his *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> defines such friendships by saying that the true friend is **another self** <note>original: "un'altro se medesimo"; a translation of the Greek *heteros autos*</note>. This is to denote that he who is in true friendship has a double life constituted in two persons: in his own and in that of his friend. Thus, his friend is another self, and each of them embraces two lives together—his own and that of his friend. With equal love, he loves both persons and likewise preserves both lives. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Philo is elaborating on the metaphysical union achieved through virtuous human friendship before transitioning to Sophia's inquiry regarding the nature of divine love.</meta>

"You shall love your neighbor as yourself" <note>original: "Amarai il prossimo come tè medesimo"; a central commandment from Leviticus 19:18.</note> requires that friendship be of such a kind that people are made equally united, and that one and the same love exists in the soul of each friend. But the falsity of this opinion is manifest, because such exterior goods are caused by interior ones, in such a way that the former depend on the latter. Furthermore, happiness must consist in the most excellent goods; this happiness is the end of all others, and is not sought for any other purpose, but rather all other things exist for its sake. Most importantly, such exterior goods are in the power of fortune, whereas happiness ought to be within the power of man.

Some others have held a different opinion, saying that blessedness consists in that which is pleasurable; these are the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus, whom Renaissance writers often (sometimes unfairly) characterized as seeking only physical pleasure and denying the immortality of the soul.</note>, who hold the mortality of the soul and believe nothing in man to be happy except for delight in whatever form it may take. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sofia, following the discussion of Aristotle's views on the human capacity for knowledge. It transitions from the idea of potential knowledge to the "act" of understanding, explaining why happiness is found in the active use of the mind rather than its mere capacity.</meta>

When he sleeps he is not happy, but when he enjoys and delights in the act of understanding, then he is happy. Therefore, if this is so, **beatitude** <note>original: "beatitudine"; the state of supreme blessedness or the highest human good.</note> necessarily consists in a single act of understanding. For although one may possess many **habits of science** <term>Habits of science: From the Latin *habitus*; a stable disposition or acquired quality of the mind that allows a person to use knowledge readily.</term> at the same time, one cannot actually understand more than one thing at once. Thus, happiness cannot consist in all things, nor in many or various known things, but must consist solely in the knowledge of a single thing. 

It is quite true that to reach beatitude, one first requires great perfection in all the sciences: first in the art of demonstrating and dividing truth from falsehood in every understanding and discourse, which is called **Logic**; then in **moral philosophy**, which involves the use of **prudence** <note>original: "prudentia"; the practical wisdom required to govern one's actions and virtues.</note> and the active virtues. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo concerning the ultimate end of human existence. the sole object of our happiness; we love Him with knowledge and love, and the wise men were divided concerning these two acts—that is, whether the proper act of happiness is to know God, or indeed to love Him. It should suffice you to know that both acts are necessary for beatitude <term>Beatitudine: Supreme blessedness or happiness, often used in a theological sense to describe the state of being in God's presence.</term>.

SO. I would like to know the reasoning that moved each of the originators of these two opinions.

PHI. Those who hold that happiness consists in loving God use this reasoning: that beatitude consists in the final act that our soul performs toward God, as that is the ultimate human end; and since it is necessary first to know Him and then to love Him, it follows that happiness consists not in knowledge, but in the love of God, which is the final act. They also support their view with the concept of delight <term>Dilettatione: Spiritual joy or pleasure derived from the fulfillment of a desire or the presence of a beloved object.</term>, which is a principal part of happiness and belongs to the will. Hence they say that the true act of happiness is voluntary—that is, love, in which delight consists—and not in the intellectual act, because it does not participate in delight in the same way.

The others, on the contrary, use this reasoning: they say that happiness consists in the act of the principal and most spiritual faculty of our soul; and since the intellectual faculty is more principal than the will and more abstracted from matter, it follows that beatitude does not consist in the act of the will, which is to love Him. Rather, they say that love and delight follow knowledge as accessories, but they are not the principal end.

SO. One reason seems no less effective to me than the other; yet I would still like to know your determination.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo (PHI.) and Sophia (SO.) regarding the nature of human happiness. The same happens with a man and a woman: by knowing her as an exemplar, she is loved and desired; and from that love, one comes to the unitive knowledge which is the end of desire. And so it is in every other loved thing

This kind of desire is called love. It concerns things not yet held that one desires to have, or truly, things already held that one desires to enjoy through union. <meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philo explains that the human intellect, when illuminated by grace, moves beyond human speculation into a transformative union with God. For this reason, Holy Scripture—after admonishing us that we must know the perfect and pure unity of God, and then that we must love Him more than the utility of greed, more than the pleasure of appetite, and more than any other virtuous good of the soul and the rational will—says as a final end: "Therefore, couple yourselves with God" <note>original: "Per tanto con esso Dio ui coppulate"; this likely refers to the biblical command to "cleave" (dveikut) to God found in Deuteronomy.</note>. This is because this "coupling" <term>Coupling: From the Italian "coppulatione," this term translates the Hebrew concept of "dveikut" (cleaving or adhesion), referring to the highest mystical union between the soul and the Creator.</term> is the most proper and precise word to signify beatitude <term>Beatitude: A state of supreme blessedness or perfect happiness, the ultimate fulfillment of the soul's nature.</term>, which contains all the good and perfection of the intellective soul, as its true happiness.

It is quite true that in this life it is not so easy to attain such beatitude; and even if one were able to attain it, it is not so easy to continue in it always. The reason for this is that while we live, our intellect has a sort of bond with the matter of this fragile body of ours. Because of this cause, anyone who has reached such coupling in this life did not remain in it constantly due to this bodily connection; instead, after that divine coupling, one would return to recognize corporeal things as before. The exception is at the end of life: the soul, remaining coupled, leaves the body entirely, remaining joined with the coupling Divinity in supreme happiness.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. The opening fragment "to da questa" completes the phrase "born from this" (Italian: *nato da questa*), responding to Sophia's question at the end of the previous page regarding whether true love is born from reason.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Philo's explanation of why love, though born from reason, eventually escapes reason's control. It follows the discussion of Cupid’s traditional attributes (blindness, nakedness, childhood).</meta>

...nor perfect union of the lover within the beloved, which cannot occur except through the total <term>penetration</term><note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "penetration" refers to the desire for two distinct entities to occupy the same space or essence simultaneously—a feat possible for spirits but impossible for physical bodies.</note> of one into the other. This is possible for souls, which are spiritual, because incorporeal spirits can, through their subtle and most effective powers, interpenetrate one another, unite, and be converted into one. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. ...[if] <term>reason</term><note>Italian: *Ragione*. But regarding <term>extraordinary reason</term><note>A higher form of logic that recognizes the beloved as more important than the self.</note>, its intent is to attain the beloved object; it does not concern itself with the preservation of one’s own interests, but rather sets them aside to acquire what is loved—just as the less noble must be set aside for the more excellent. Thus, it is reasonable to labor for that which is greater. You can understand this through both a **natural example** and a **moral example**. 

**Naturally**, you will see a man about to be struck in the head; he instinctively puts forward his arm to save his head, because the head is more noble. Likewise, since the lover and the beloved have become one, and the beloved is the more noble part of this union while the lover is the less noble, the lover naturally does not shy away from any affliction or pain to attain the beloved. With every care and diligence, the lover follows the beloved as their true end, abandoning all that belongs to themselves as if it belonged to another. 

The **moral example** is this: just as "first reason" commands us to preserve our wealth for our own needs so that we may live well and comfortably, the "second reason" commands us to dispense that wealth generously to others for a more noble end—namely, to acquire the **virtue** of <term>liberality</term><note>In Renaissance philosophy, liberality (Italian: *liberalità*) was the virtue of being noble and generous with one's wealth, finding the "golden mean" between greed and wastefulness.</note>.

<summary>Philo argues that "perfect love" follows a higher form of reason that prioritizes the beloved (the "end") over the self (the "means"). SOPHIA: May God save you, Philo. Do you pass by like this without speaking?

PHILO: The enemy of my well-being <note>original: "salute," which in Italian carries the double meaning of health/well-being and spiritual salvation</note> greets me; yet may God save you, Sophia. What do you want from me?

Thus, air and fire—which due to their proximity receive more of the heat and <term>celestial benefit</term><note>original: "beneficio celeste." In this manner, since it cannot sustain all forms together in actuality, it receives them all successively, one after another. ...all in all, and they are divided only in their form and in the path of their motion. For this reason, the head and the feet of the Heaven, which are the two poles—since neither ever changes into the other—are materially divided, just as they are in animals.

**SO.** If the East and West are one and the same, it follows that the right and left are also one and the same.

**PHI.** It is not so; for although a specific part of the Heaven may materially be the East for some and the West for others, nevertheless, according to the motion made by the whole Heaven and every part, it is East to all when it is found in its [own] East. And by the path of its motion, it is always the right and never the left. For the Heaven never moves, nor do any of its parts, in a direction contrary to that rightward motion—or rather, in reverse, as the **wandering planets** <note>original: "Pianeti erratici"; these are the planets known to the ancients (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, plus the Sun and Moon) which appear to move independently against the background of the fixed stars.</note> always do. For this reason, their motion is "leftward," and they move thus in reverse to counteract the rightward celestial motion, in order to favor the lower opposites and to cause their continual **generation** <term>generation<gloss>In this context, "generation" refers to the process of birth and the creation of physical matter, which was believed to be influenced by the movements of the planets.</gloss></term>.

P H I. The ancient Poets did not weave just one, but many intentions into their poems, which they call "senses." First of all, they provide the literal sense <term>literal sense: the basic, surface-level meaning of a story</term> as an outer rind <note>original: *scorza exteriore*</note>. This consists of the history of certain people and their notable actions, worthy of memory. Then, within that same fiction, they place—like a more internal rind, closer to the marrow <note>original: *medolla*; the pith or kernel of a fruit, used here to mean the deeper core meaning</note>—the moral sense, which is useful for the active life of men by praising virtuous acts and condemning vices. Beyond this, beneath those very words, they signify some true understanding of natural or celestial things—whether astrological or truly theological. Sometimes two, or even all three of these scientific <note>original: *scientifichi*; here meaning branches of structured knowledge or scholarship</note> senses are included within the fable, like the marrow of the fruit inside its rinds. These "marrowy" senses are called allegorical.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. Because he was virtuous, he was exalted by men even to the Heavens. 

Morally, Perseus also signifies the prudent man, a son of Jove, endowed with his virtues; by killing the base and earthly vice signified by Gorgon, he ascended to the Heaven of virtue. 

Allegorically, it signifies first that the human mind, the daughter of Jove, by killing and conquering the earthliness of the "Gorgonic" nature, ascended to understand celestial, high, and eternal things; it is in this contemplation <note>original: *speculatione*; in a Renaissance context, this refers to deep intellectual study or meditation on divine truths</note> that human perfection consists. This allegory is "natural" because man belongs to the world of natural things. 

It also seeks to signify another celestial allegory: that celestial nature, the daughter of Jove, having caused mortality and corruption in the lower earthly bodies through its continuous motion, this same celestial nature—victorious over corruptible things—breaking away from...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philo explains to Sophia why the ancient "poetic theologians" hid deep truths behind myths. He has just compared the concealment of knowledge to keeping fine wine in a clean vessel to avoid corruption.</meta>

...poetic <note>original: *[poe]tico*</note> they included the secrets of **intellectual cognition** <term>intellectual cognition: the highest form of understanding, which deals with abstract truths and divine concepts rather than physical objects</term> within **fabulous rinds** <note>original: *scorze fabulose*; a metaphor for the outer, "mythic" layer of a story that protects the inner truth</note> with the greatest artifice. **SO.** I like this reasoning: that high and excellent things should be entrusted to high and clear minds, and not be debased by those who are not so. But tell me the other reasons for these **poetic fictions** <note>original: *figmenti poetici*</note>.

**PHI.** They did so for four other reasons. The first and second are for the sake of **brevity** <note>original: *breuità*</note>, so that they might infold many meanings into a few words. This brevity is very useful for the preservation of things in the **memory** <note>original: *memoria*</note>, especially when done with such artifice that, by remembering a **historical** <note>original: *historiografo*; refers to the literal narrative or "story" level of a myth</note> event, one might also remember all the doctrinal senses included within those words.

The third reason is to mix the delight of the historical and fabulous with the intellectual truth, and the easy with the difficult. Thus, human fragility—being first enticed by the pleasure and ease of the fable—might allow the truth of **knowledge** <note>original: *scientia*</note> to enter the mind with sagacity. This is the way children are usually taught in matters of discipline and virtue, beginning with the easiest things. This is especially effective because both can exist together: the one in the "rind" and the other in the **marrow** <note>original: *medolla*; the inner essence or "pith" of the allegory</note>, as is found in **poetic fictions** <note>original: *fintioni poetiche*</note>. 

The fourth reason is for the preservation of intellectual things, so that they do not become altered over the course of time in the diverse minds of men. By placing such meanings under these histories, they cannot vary from the terms...

<summary>Philo outlines four reasons why ancients used allegory: to protect truth from the unworthy, to use brevity as a memory aid, to entice students by mixing pleasure with difficult study, and to prevent the corruption of knowledge over time.</summary>

Thus, he was the first who broke part of the law regarding the preservation of knowledge; yet he left it enclosed within a **mythic style** <note>original: *stile fabuloso*</note> in such a way that it sufficed for its preservation. **Aristotle**, more daring and eager for expansion, with a new and distinct manner and style of expression, also wished to remove the lock of the fable and completely break the law of preservation. It is quite true, however, that he employed such marvelous skill—speaking so briefly, so comprehensively, and with such profound meaning—that it sufficed for the preservation of the sciences in place of verse and fable. This was so much the case that in his response to **Alexander of Macedon**, his pupil—who had written to him in wonder that he had revealed such secret books of **sacred Philosophy**—he replied that his books were **published and yet not published** <note>original: *editi, et non editi*</note>. They were published only to those who had learned their meaning directly from him. From these words, O **Sophia**, you will note the difficulty and the craft inherent in **Aristotle's** way of speaking. **SOPHIA**. I [it]...

And the Greeks called him **Zeus** <note>original: *Zefs*; Philo connects the name to the Greek word for life, *zoe*</note>, which means **life**, because from him all things have life—indeed, he is the life of every thing. It is quite true that this name "Jupiter" was shared by the omnipotent God with some of his most excellent creatures. In the celestial world, this name fell to the second of the seven planets, called **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter (planet): in ancient astrology, this planet is known as the "Greater Benefic," believed to be the most naturally helpful and lucky of the wandering stars</term>, because it is the greater fortune, possessing the clearest splendor and the most excellent effects on the lower world; it is the planet that produces the best, most excellent, and most fortunate men through its constellation and influence. In the lower world, the **elemental Fire** is also called Jupiter, for being the clearest and most active of all the elements, acting as the life of all lower things which (according to **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle argued in *On Youth and Old Age* that life is maintained by "vital heat"</note>) live by means of heat. In this way, the poetic fictions <note>The author uses "fictions" not to mean "lies," but rather "constructed allegories" meant to convey truth.</note> of heroic men called Gods multiplied. For when they narrate their lives, deeds, and history, they signify matters of **moral philosophy**; when they name them after virtues, vices, and passions, they signify matters of **natural philosophy**; by naming them after the inferior Gods of the world, and of generation and corruption, they demonstrate **astrology** and the **science of the heavens**; and by naming them with the names of the celestial Gods, they signify the **theology** of God and of the Angels. Thus, these fictions were ingenious and full of high wisdom in their manifold naming of the Gods.

For this reason, the Poets call the formal principle the **Giving Father** and the material principle the **Receiving Mother**. In order for these two principles to work together to bring anything into being, it was necessary for them to love one another and be joined through **love** <note>original: "amore"</note> to produce the new creation, just as human and animal parents do. The ancients posited this matter as coeternal with God, and from it He (when it pleased Him) generated all created things, as the true father of all; thus matter is the common mother of every generated being. In this way, they posit only these two parents of all things—one the father and the other the mother—as eternal and <term>ungenerated</term> <note>original: "ignatī." He was called this for being so excellent in virtue and possessed of such profound intellect that he seemed celestial and worthy of being the son of Aether and Dies; for he shared in the ethereal spirituality in his intellect and the divine light in his virtue. 

The allegory of this is quite manifest, because the Heavens, which surround everything, conceal <note>The author is making an etymological pun: in Italian, *Cielo* (Heaven) sounds like *cela* (conceals).</note> and cover all things. However, the shining bodies <note>The stars and planets.</note> are specific members of the Heavens in the same way the Female is a part of the Man, who represents the whole. This is also because Aether is a more subtle and spiritual body than the shining bodies of the **Stars** and **Planets**. For this reason, **Aristotle** says that because the Stars are of a thicker and denser corporeality than the rest of the Heavens, they are capable of receiving and holding light within themselves—something the sphere <note>original: "orbe".</note> cannot do because of its transparent subtlety. Plotinus maintains that the subtlety of Aether is so great that it penetrates all bodies of the universe, thus supe- <note>The text breaks off mid-word; "supe-" likely continues as "superiore" (superior) or "superficie" (surface) on the next page.</note>

Mars and Venus were freed, for which reason Venus always thereafter hated the Sun and all his progeny; because of this, she caused all his daughters to commit adultery.

**SO.** What do you say then, O Philo, of such great lewdness and adultery among the celestial Gods?

**PHI.** The allegory of this fable is not only scholarly <note>original: "scientifica"; in this period, it refers to knowledge based on philosophical and natural principles.</note> but also useful, because it demonstrates that the excess of carnal lewdness not only damns all the powers and virtues of the human body, but also causes a defect in that very act, with a diminution of the ordinary.

**SO.** Explain it to me at length.

**PHI.** Venus is the concupiscible appetite <note>The faculty of the soul that desires physical pleasures and sensory gratification.</note> of man, which derives from the planet Venus; according to the efficacy of her influence in nativities <note>A person's astrological birth chart.</note>, this appetite is great and intense. This Venus is married to Vulcan, who is the God of the lower Fire; in man, this is his natural heat <term>Natural heat (Calor naturale): A fundamental concept in Renaissance medicine, referring to the internal biological heat that fuels digestion, growth, and reproduction.</term> which limits and puts concupiscence into action. As her husband, he is always actually joined to her. Of the four causes of natural things—which are the material, the formal, the agent cause <term>agent cause</term><note>Also known as the efficient cause; the person or force that acts to produce an effect.</note> (which makes or moves the thing), and the final cause (which is the end that moves the agent to act)—of all these, the material is the lowest. The formal is better than the material, and the agent is better and more noble than both because it is the cause of them. But the final cause is the most noble and excellent of all four, and more so than the agent cause, because the agent moves itself for the sake of the end. 

Whence the end is called the "cause of all causes." From this it is concluded that the end for which the intellectual Soul of each of the Heavens moves its orb is of greater excellence not only than the Body of the Heaven, but even than the Soul itself.

# SOPHIA AND PHILO ON THE ORIGIN OF LOVE

**SO.** Philo, oh Philo, do you not hear, or do you not wish to answer?

**SO.** Do not pass by in such a hurry; listen a moment.

**PHI.** Indeed, that part is worth no more in me than in anyone else, nor is it esteemed by me more than it ought to be; nor are these present needs of such importance that they could so deeply withdraw my soul—so the things for which I was going are not the causes of my alienation <note>alienatione: a state of being mentally "elsewhere" or lost in thought, often used in Renaissance philosophy to describe the soul leaving the senses to contemplate higher truths</note> (as you think).

**SO.** If I knew it, I would not ask you; since I ask, I must not know. 

**PHI.** If you do not know, you ought to know.

In this way, the predecessor of hearing is sight; and commonly, the ear depends upon the eye as the principal origin of intellectual knowledge. The other three senses are entirely corporeal, made more for the recognition and use of things necessary for the sustenance of the animal <note>Here, "animal" refers to the biological life of the body.</note> than for intellectual knowledge.

In this context, it refers to substances like air or water that allow light to pass through them without being permanently changed.</note></term> transparent bodies, such as Air and Water, the Light of the illuminating source manifests as a separable spiritual act, and not in a corporeal way as a quality or passion; and the diaphanous medium is merely a vehicle for the Light, but not its subject. **SOPHIA.** Why not? **PHILO.** Because if light in a diaphanous medium were a quality within a subject, it would have the conditions of such a quality, which are six in number. First, because a quality would spread through the whole subject one part after another, but light penetrates the entire diaphanous medium instantaneously. Second, an incoming quality changes the natural disposition of its subject, but Light causes no change in the diaphanous medium. Third, because quality extends to a limited space, but Light extends through the diaphanous medium without limit or measure. Fourth, because when the source that forms the quality is removed, that quality always remains for some time

So it is that the true light is the intellectual light, which essentially illuminates the corporeal and incorporeal World; and in man, it gives light to the Soul and to **intellectual vision** <note>The capacity for spiritual or rational understanding, as opposed to physical sight.</note>. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo, moving from a general comparison of the human intellect and the Sun to a specific technical discussion of the optics of vision. ...all the other <term>cognitive powers<note>original: "uirtu conofcitiue"; refers to the various faculties of the soul, such as memory, imagination, and perception, that allow a human to know the world.</note></term> of man; so that although their knowledge is particular and material, it may be directed by the intellect—not in a bestial way, as in other animals. And yet, the eye and the Sun are not so similar, for the eye sees and does not illuminate, while the Sun illuminates and does not see. 

PHI. Perhaps in this they are not so dissimilar; for our eye not only sees by means of the universal illumination of the <term>diaphanous medium<note>original: "diaphano"; in Renaissance science, this refers to a transparent substance like air or water that allows light to pass through.</note></term>, but also with the particular illumination of <term>luminous rays<note>original: "raggi lucidi"</note></term> that issue from the eye itself and reach out to the object. While these rays alone are not sufficient to illuminate the medium and the object, nonetheless, without them, the universal light would not be enough to make <term>vision<note>original: "uifione"</note></term> actual. 

SO. Do you believe, then, that the eye sees by sending its rays into the object? 

PHI. Yes, I believe so. 

SO. In this you are no longer a <term>Peripatetic<note>original: "Peripatetico"; a follower of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note></term>, for <term>Aristotle<note>The influential Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose theories of physics and logic dominated European thought for centuries.</note></term> rejects this and holds that vision occurs through the representation of the <term>species<note>original: "spetie de l'oggetto"; in this context, the "species" is the formal image or likeness of an object transmitted through the air to the eye.</note></term> of the object within the <term>pupil<note>original: "pupilla"</note></term> of the eye, and not by sending out rays as <term>Plato<note>The Greek philosopher (c. 428–348 BCE) who proposed that the eye emits a "visual fire" or rays to perceive the world.</note></term> says. 

PHI. Aristotle did not prove the case against Plato, because I hold that in the act of seeing both things are necessary: both the emission of rays from the eye to seize and illuminate the object, and the representation of the species of the object in the pupil. And even these two contrary movements are not enough for vision without a third and final one, which is the eye—by means of the rays upon the object—acting secondarily to conform the received species of the object with the external object; and in this third act consists the perfect logic of vision. 

SO. This [theory] of yours seems new to me...

<summary>In this passage, Philo argues for a hybrid theory of vision, combining Plato's idea that the eye emits rays with Aristotle's idea that the eye receives images (species), suggesting that vision requires a three-part process to reconcile the internal image with the external world.</summary>

Therefore for two days the Moon is not visible to us, nor on the other days of the month is the illumination of the half of the Moon's sphere <note>original: "palla de la Luna," literally "ball of the moon"</note> consistent, because from the **conjunction** <term>conjunction (coniunctione): The moment when the Moon and Sun are aligned, making the Moon invisible from Earth (the New Moon).</term> the light begins to diminish from the upper part and move toward the lower part facing us little by little, as it moves away from the **Sun** <note>original: "Sole"</note>. Afterward, the light begins to transfer back to the upper part, decreasing little by little in the part facing us until it reaches the upper part; at that time, our entire side lacks light, and the upper side—which we do not see—is entirely bright.

**PHILO.** Since the highest and most perfect beauty exists within the **divine intellect**, the soul—which is a splendor proceeding from that intellect—falls in love with that supreme intellectual beauty, its superior origin, just as the imperfect female falls in love with the male who brings her to perfection <note>In the philosophical tradition of this period, the "male" was often associated with active form and perfection, while the "female" was associated with receptive matter and potentiality.</note>; and she desires to find happiness in her perpetual union with it. <meta>This page continues the Dialogue of Love. Philo and Sophia are engaged in a sophisticated rhetorical debate, using the language of commerce and legal obligation—"debt," "promises," and "grace"—to negotiate their emotional and intellectual exchange. Philo is attempting to prioritize Sophia's moral duty to pity his suffering over his own previous promise to explain the nature of Love.</meta>

...debts in your way would be neither to pay nor to grant a favor <note>original: "gratia," referring to a gift given freely rather than out of obligation</note>, for I see that you are trying to sell anew what you have already promised. **PHI.** To help friends as much as possible—does that not seem a debt to you?

**SO.** Even if that were a debt, you will not deny that among debts, a promised one must be paid before one that was not promised.

**PHI.** I will not grant you this either; for by reason, one should first pay what is a debt in its own right <note>Philo argues that moral duties inherent in friendship are more fundamental than verbal contracts.</note> without being promised, rather than that which is only made a debt by a promise. Indeed, a debt without a promise takes precedence over a promise without a debt. See how providing a **remedy** for my terrible suffering is a true debt (since we are true friends), even though you have not promised it. But my promise was not made out of debt, but rather out of favor, nor is it very necessary for you, since it is not intended to rescue you from danger or harm, but only to give you some delight and mental satisfaction. Therefore, your unpromised debt should take precedence over my freely given promise.

**SO.** A promise alone is what creates a debt, without the need for any other obligation.

**PHI.** It is more just that the debt itself should imply a promise, without any need for the act of promising.

**SO.** Even if it were so—

<meta>This page continues the Dialogue of Love. Philo has been arguing that Sophia owes him a "debt of pity" for the suffering his love for her causes. ...as you say, do you not see that what I want from you is the **theory** of love, and what you want from me is the **practice** of it? His greatness is worthy of praise, but his fierce operations—especially toward me—are worthy of blame.

<meta>This page continues Philo’s summary of Sophia’s five questions regarding the origin of Love. Having previously discussed whether Love is born, when, and where, he now moves to the identity of Love's parents and the purpose of his existence.</meta>

...mind of both <note>Philo is likely completing the fourth point: from whose mind or union Love was born.</note> he was born, and who they were—whether divine, or human, or truly of some other nature—and furthermore, what their genealogy was. ...which is to desire things that are lacking; because that which is possessed, while it is possessed, is not craved nor loved <note>Philo is making a technical distinction: one does not "desire" what they already hold, yet they "love" the prospect of keeping it.</note>, but it is always loved and craved because it exists in the mind as a kind of good thing. Thus, one desires and loves it—if it does not yet really exist—so that it may exist in reality, just as it does in the mind; that is, that it may be **in act** <note>original: "in atto" — a philosophical term meaning a thing has achieved its full reality, as opposed to just being a possibility.</note>, as it is **in potential** <note>original: "in potentia" — the capacity or possibility for something to exist.</note>. This future enjoyment does not yet exist and is therefore "lacking." In this way, a father and son love each other, desiring to enjoy one another's presence in the future just as they do in the present. Similarly, the healthy man loves health, and the rich man loves riches; he does not only desire that they increase, but also that he may enjoy them in the future just as he does now. Therefore, love—just like desire—must be directed toward things that are in some way lacking. This is why Plato defines love as the **appetite** <note>original: "appetito" — a natural drive or craving toward a goal.</note> for a good thing in order to possess it, and to do so forever; for in that "forever," a continuous lack is included.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia regarding the definitions of love and desire. Philo is explaining how linguistic distinctions (using "love" for noble things and "desire" for lesser things) often mask the fact that they are essentially the same impulse. The previous page ended with Philo beginning an example about how specific names are often derived from general concepts.</meta>

<sig>HHH</sig>

the universal name for everything desired is applied to persons, or to principal things that have in themselves a more stable **existence** <note>original: "essere più fermo" — referring to things that are enduring or substantial.</note>, and of other things we say we desire them, and not love them, because their existence is weaker. But in effect, all things are loved; for even if I do not say that I love a thing that does not yet exist, I will say that I love for it *to be*, and if I do not have it, that I love *to have it*. This is still the true intention of the one who desires when they desire—that is, if it is not desiring that it *be*, then it is desiring *to have it*. Nevertheless, "love," as a more excellent word, is applied primarily to persons who exist, and to excellent things that bring **perfection** <note>original: "perfettive" — things that complete or improve one’s nature, like wisdom or health.</note>, or rather to things already possessed. For others, we would sooner use the words <term>appetere</term> (to crave), <term>optare</term> (to wish), and <term>desiare</term> (to desire), rather than to love, nor <term>affettare</term> (to aspire to), nor <term>diligere</term> (to esteem or choose), because these latter terms usually indicate a more noble and stable object. Commonly, love is applied to the things themselves, and desire to the actions of their being or of having them, despite the fact that in substance the meaning is one and the same.

<meta>This page continues the third dialogue of Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues of Love." <meta>This page continues the third dialogue of Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues of Love." **SO.** In what way? Likewise, the teacher desires virtue and wisdom for the student—qualities which are lacking in the student, not the teacher. <meta>This page continues the discussion between Philo and Sophia in Leone Ebreo's "Dialogues of Love." Philo is clarifying the nature of divine love by distinguishing his definition from Plato’s. He argues that while Plato defines love as a desire for beauty (which implies the lover lacks beauty), a broader definition of love allows for God to love His creatures by desiring their well-being without God Himself being "deficient" or "lacking" in any way.</meta>

...nor can it exist in God; but regarding the universal love of which we speak, it would be false to deny that it exists in God. 

**SO.** Explain this difference to me. 

**PHI.** Plato, in his *Symposium* <note>original: "Simphosio" — Plato's famous philosophical dialogue regarding the nature and origins of Love.</note>, discusses only that kind of love found in humans which is centered on the lover <note>original: "terminato ne l'amante" — meaning the love is directed toward satisfying the lover's own needs or desires.</note>, but not on the beloved. For this is what is primarily called "love," whereas that which is centered on the beloved is called "friendship" and "benevolence." 

He rightly defines this kind of love as the "desire for beauty." He says such love is not found in God, because whoever desires beauty does not possess it, nor is he beautiful; and since God is the <term>supreme beauty</term> <note>original: "sommo bello" — the highest form of beauty, which in Neoplatonic thought is synonymous with God or the Divine.</note>, He does not lack beauty, nor can He desire it. Therefore, God cannot have love—at least, not of that specific kind. 

But we, who speak of love in a general sense, must equally include both the love centered on the lover—which presupposes a <term>deficiency</term> <note>original: "mancamento" — a central theme in this work; the idea that love stems from a "lack" of something the lover wants to possess.</note> in the lover—and the love centered on the beloved, which presupposes a deficiency in the beloved, but not in the lover. 

For this reason, we have not defined love as the "desire for a beautiful thing" (as Plato did), but simply as the "desire for something," or rather, the "desire for a good thing." This "good" may be something the Lover lacks, or it may be something that only the Beloved lacks—as is the case with the love of a father for his son, a teacher for his student, or a friend for a friend. Such is the love of God for His creatures: a desire for *their* good, not His own. And of this...

<summary>Philo distinguishes his "universal love" from Plato's definition, arguing that love can be a desire for the beloved's well-being rather than just a lover's attempt to fill a personal void. This allows for a model of divine love where God desires the perfection of His creatures without lacking anything Himself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Philo's explanation of Aristotelian cosmology. ...impassible and immutable in substance and quality; and its round figure, among all other shapes, is the only one free from contrariety <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "contrariety" refers to opposing qualities like hot and cold or up and down. Because a circle has no opposite points or directions, it was considered perfect and unchanging.</note>. Consequently, circular motion is incompatible with having a beginning; for just as the circular shape—which is the celestial shape—has no beginning, and every point within it is both beginning and end, so too is circular motion without a beginning, and every part of it is both a beginning and an end. 

Furthermore, regarding the first motion <note>The "first motion" refers to the movement of the highest celestial sphere, which was thought to set the rest of the universe in motion.</note>: if it were generated, then its "generation" (which is itself a motion) would have to exist before the first motion, which is impossible. Since one cannot have an infinite chain of preceding motions, one must arrive at an eternal first motion. Moreover, time—which follows the first motion, as it is the measurement of the "before" and "after" of motion—must be eternal just as motion is. This is because every instant is effectively the end of past time and the beginning of future time, such that no specific instant can be designated as the absolute first beginning. Time is, therefore, eternal, without ever having had a beginning.

**SO.** I understand the reasons that moved **Aristotle** to make prime matter and the Heaven eternal in themselves, and the generation of things, circular motion, and time eternal in a successive manner, one part following after another. **PHI.** These that I have told you are his natural reasons. <meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. On the previous page, Sophia questioned whether matter could exist in time before taking a form. Philo now contrasts Aristotle's view (that the world is eternal but the heavens have a different kind of "matter") with Plato's view (that everything, including the heavens, is formed from the same underlying unformed matter).</meta>

How then does Aristotle maintain that the formed World is eternal?

**PHILO.** Because he does not posit prime matter <term>prime matter: the fundamental, formless substance that is the "subject" of all physical change</term> as common to the whole World, but only in the lower world of generation and corruption <note>generation and corruption: the philosophical terms for the birth/creation and death/decay of physical things on Earth.</note>. In that lower world, he posits that prime matter is eternal and that no single form is coeternal with it; instead, each form is new within it through generation, and another is reborn through corruption. He posits that the succession of many and diverse forms is eternal, through eternal generation and corruption, yet each of those forms is individually new, generable, and corruptible.

**SOPHIA.** In the heavens then, where there is no generation, will Aristotle not posit matter?

**PHILO.** In no way. He does not want the Heavens and Stars to have substantial matter, because if they had it, they would be generable and corruptible like the lower bodies. Instead, they are only an eternal body, which is "matter" for movement, but not for generation <note>Aristotle argued the heavens were made of a fifth element (aether) that only changed by moving in circles, never by changing its actual substance.</note>.

**SOPHIA.** And Plato—why does he not posit eternal matter as eternally informed, and successively shaped by successive forms?

Against that opinion, the strongest of its arguments have no place, such as the claim that nothing is made from nothing and that **prime matter** <term>Prime matter (materia prima)</term><note>The fundamental, formless substance that underlies all physical reality in Aristotelian and Platonic thought.</note> cannot be newly made or generated. **Plato** himself grants and presupposes those propositions, as well as those two theological arguments concerning the divine work: that it must be eternal, like its **Maker** <term>Opifice</term><note>Referring to God as the Divine Architect or Craftsman (Demiurge).</note>, and thus that the end [purpose] of His work, which is good, must be eternal. Plato grants both these propositions insofar as they pertain to the divine agent.

But he says that God bestows His eternity upon that which is capable of enjoying it, such as the **Intellect**, in which the **Ideas** reside, and **prime matter**, which is **Chaos**. For the one is pure act and form, and the other is pure potentiality and matter entirely unformed; the one is the universal father of all things, and the other the common Mother to all. Only these have been able to participate in the divine eternity, having been produced by Him from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note>. But their children—who are made and formed by God through these two parents, as is the whole universe and each of its parts—are not capable of eternity, because every thing that is made is "formed," that is, composed of matter...

**PHI.** Plato does not concede to Aristotle that Chaos can be found without form; rather, he says that after having germinated for a long time, it gathers all things back into itself and rests for a certain interval of time, becoming "pregnant" with the Ideas, until it then returns to give birth and germinate the universe anew. He grants that generation is eternal in many successive cycles, but not in a single version of the **Heaven** <note>The celestial sphere. While Aristotle believed the heavens were eternal and unchanging, the Plato described here suggests even the heavens are part of a cycle of dissolution and rebirth.</note>; for the "contrariety" by which it dissolves is the very fact of being formed, made, and composed of matter and form. Because every such thing must eventually dissolve, its **circular motion** <note>The movement of the stars and planets, which ancient philosophers used to measure time.</note> must cease. Although motion in a universal sense is eternal through the eternal successive germination of Chaos, and as for **time**, he says it is eternal—not because of the motion of the Heaven, but because of the eternal, successive germinative motion of Chaos.

**SO.** I am quite pleased with the solution to Aristotle’s arguments on Plato’s behalf, and very

...corporeal nature, I do not know how it can be called infinite. 

**PHILO.** Do not let the specific property of the word *infinite* mislead you, which signifies an indeterminate and imperfect quantity—from which divine beauty is very distant. However, we cannot speak of God and of incorporeal things except in words that are somewhat corporeal, because our very language and speech is in itself corporeal. Furthermore, even the word **perfect** is an inadequate term for the divinity, because it literally means "entirely made" <note>Philo is referencing the Latin root *perfectus*, from *per-* (completely) and *facere* (to do/make). He argues that because God was never "made" or created, the word is technically a misfit.</note>, and in the divinity there is no "making" or creation at all. But by **perfect**, we mean that which is deprived of every defect and which contains every perfection; and by **infinite**, we mean that the perfection, wisdom, and beauty of God the Creator is disproportionate and incomparable to any created perfection. 

Since He who created everything from nothing must exceed His creatures in perfection—creatures who in themselves are nothing—as much as the <term>Supreme Being</term> <note>God, as the ultimate source of all existence.</note> exceeds pure nothingness. This is an <term>incommensurable excess</term> <note>A difference so vast it cannot be measured or compared using the same scale.</note> without any proportion or comparison, which we call **infinite**, although in itself it is most whole and most perfect. 

Furthermore, divine beauty, wisdom, being, and every virtue are called **infinite** because they are not restricted to any specific essence, nor to any finite subject; rather, all the perfections in Him are most abstract, **transcendent**, and infinite, because they are not limited by a specific subject or essence, just as the being and beauty of every created thing is limited by its own essence.
