**PHILO.** The imagination must not hinder **reason**, especially in those like you, Sophia. You see clearly that the infinite is immeasurable by any kind of measure, large or small; for if it were measured by any, it would be finished by that measure, and would no longer be infinite. Wherefore, one can never assign a half, a third, a fourth, or any other part to the infinite, because it would then be measured by that part. It is, therefore, impartible, indivisible, and immeasurable, without limit and without end; and no finite thing, however great and excellent it may be, is proportionate to it in any kind of proportion. 

**SOPHIA.** Give me some example, so that my imagination may be better satisfied. 

**PHILO.** Time, according to the **philosophers**, is infinite: it had no beginning, nor will it ever have an end—though we who are faithful <note>Philo refers to the religious doctrine of creation, which holds that the universe had a beginning, contrary to the Aristotelian view that the world and time are eternal.</note> hold the contrary. But according to those philosophers, time, being infinite, is incommensurable by any quantity of finite time, whether large or small. Thus, it is just as disproportionate and incommensurable by a thousand years as it is by one hour; so that in infinite time, there is no fewer a number of thousands of...

**SOPHIA:** What does he wish to signify?

**PHILO:** The ordinary commentaries <note>Philo refers here to the standard literal or rabbinic interpretations which attempt to harmonize the two creation accounts in Genesis (Chapter 1 and Chapter 2).</note> struggle literally to reconcile this text, saying that first he spoke of the creation of both in summary, and then he gives the method in detail, describing how the woman was made from the man's side. **SOPHIA:** What, then, do you mean to signify by this opposition of words?

**PHILO:** It means that **Adam**—that is, the first human, whom God created on the sixth day of creation—being a single human individual <term>supposto</term> <note>original: "supposto." Therefore, it says that God created **Adam** in the image of God; "male and female He created them." At one point the text calls him in the singular, "**Adam**," one man; at another point, it calls them in the plural, "male and female He created them," to denote that, while being one individual, he contained both male and female together. For this reason, the ancient Hebrew commentaries in the Chaldean language <note>original: "lingua caldea." The text clarifies this at the end, saying that God created **Adam** male and female and "called their name **Adam**," which declares that the name **Adam** alone contained both, and that at first, the single individual made of both was called **Adam**. Indeed, the female was never called **Eve** until she was divided from her male, **Adam**. From this account, **Plato** and the Greeks took their concept of the ancient **Androgyne** <note>original: "Androgeno." From the Greek *androgynos* (man-woman), a being possessing both male and female characteristics.</note>, half-male and half-female.

This means it did not seem right for **Adam** to remain male and female in a single body, joined at the back with faces turned away from each other; rather, it was better that his female part be divided and come in front of him, face to face, so she could be a helper to him. PHILO: The human as male joined with female (as I have told you) had no way to sin, because the serpent could not deceive the woman while she was joined with the man, as it later did once she was separated from him. Immediately thereafter, it narrates the incision of **Adam** into divided male and female; and once the division was made, it immediately describes the deception of the serpent, and the sin of **Adam** and **Eve**, and their punishment.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical explanation of Plato’s myth of the Androgyne, exploring why the original unified human being was divided. Philo explains that this division was necessary to balance man's spiritual nature with his physical survival, leading to the birth of Love as a unifying force.</meta>

...being entirely angelic, it corrupted the human composition, individual preservation, and the succession of the species <note>The author argues that if humans were purely intellectual/angelic, they would neglect their physical bodies and fail to reproduce, leading to the extinction of the human race.</note>. This is the "fight against the gods" that **Plato** mentions. Therefore, he <note>Jupiter, representing the divine will.</note> had them divided; that is, he caused the body to offer some resistance to the intellect, and the intellect to incline toward the necessary cares and natural needs of the body, so that life might be human rather than purely angelic. 

He says that from this division, **Love** was born, because every half desires and loves the reintegration of its remaining half. This means, in effect, that the intellect would never care for the body if it were not for the love it has for its consort—the feminine, corporeal half. Likewise, the body would not be governed by the intellect if not for the love and affection it has for its consort—the masculine, intellectual half. 

Furthermore, regarding his statement that when one half joined with the other, they sought nothing necessary for their sustenance out of love and thus perished: as a remedy, **Jupiter** turned their genitals toward one another. Once they were satisfied through <term>coitus</term> <note>Sexual intercourse.</note> and the generation of their like <note>The procreation of children.</note>, their division was reintegrated. This signifies that the purpose of the division of the intellectual and corporeal parts was so that, by finding satisfaction in corporeal delights, they might sustain themselves as individuals and produce offspring for the perpetual preservation of the species. 

He then warns that one must not sin, lest each half of man be divided again, leaving only a quarter of a man. By this, he means that if the intellectual part is not united but remains divided by imperfect cognitions and counsels, it remains imperfect...

The division prevents humans from being purely "angelic" and encourages the preservation of the species through the balance of spirit and body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the myth of the birth of Love from Plato’s Symposium, transitioning from the description of Porus and Penia to a philosophical explanation of the "possible intellect" in human nature.</meta>

the rose of perfection became pregnant by him, who was intoxicated by the desire for corporeal perfection, half-asleep from his eternal divine contemplation, and diverted somewhat from that state in order to share perfection with needy matter. From both of them Love was born, because Love signifies perfection not in act, but in potentiality <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" is something fully realized, while "potentiality" is the capacity to become something.</note>. Thus, the intellect within the generable body—which is potential form and the <term>possible intellect (the human capacity for thought that is not yet fully realized)</term>—is born. Because it is an intellect, it recognizes beautiful things; but because it exists only in potentiality, it lacks the possession of them and desires actual beauty. 

This is what is meant by saying that Love is halfway between the beautiful and the ugly, because the possible intellect and material forms are halfway between pure matter (which is totally formless) and the separate forms and actual angelic intelligences, which are truly beautiful. Therefore, Diotima <note>The wise woman from Plato’s Symposium who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love.</note> assigns to Love equally the conditions and workings of needy corporeal matter—its mortal, variable, and imperfect mother—and the intellectual and perfect conditions of the affluent intellect Porus, its father. She presents Love as a "philosopher" <note>original: "filosofante". Literally "one who philosophizes." In the original Greek sense, a philosopher is a lover of wisdom who does not yet possess it fully, unlike a "wise man" who already knows.</note> and not a wise man, because the possible intellect desires wisdom and has the potential for it, but it is not actually wise like the angelic intellect. 

Diotima thus showed in this fable of hers that the possible intellect participates in the <term>agent intellect (the "active" power of thought)</term>—whether that be angelic or truly divine—and that its "possibility" (or potentiality) does not come from its own intellectual nature (as some believe) but only from its association with needy matter, which is deprived of all action and is pure potentiality.

**SO.** Explain to me how pregnancy and the desire to give birth to beauty exist in each of these types of love, and why such generations are so greatly desired.

Since individual animals cannot be perpetual (as **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle argued in *On the Soul* that living things reproduction is the way they participate in the eternal and the divine.</note> says), they desire and strive to perpetuate themselves through the generation of their like. They often strive for the life and being of their offspring more than their own, because it seems to them that their own life is already passing, while the offspring is that part of them that is yet to be, making their life immortal through continuous and similar succession. 

Furthermore, these goals occur in the **human soul** <term>Anima humana: The rational soul, which in this philosophy is "pregnant" with divine ideas and virtues.</term>. Being pregnant with beauty, virtue, and intellectual **wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia"</note>, the soul always desires to generate similar beauties in virtuous acts and wise habits; for through the true generation of these, true immortality is acquired. In this way, it is better than the way animated bodies acquire it through the generation of like...

...marvel, oh Sophia, that beauty is what makes every beloved, beloved, and every lover, a lover, and that it is the beginning, middle, and end of every love. Because the **First Beauty** <note>A Neoplatonic term for God, the source of all aesthetic and moral perfection.</note> is the **Supreme Architect** <term>Sommo opifice: Literally "highest craftsman," a term used to describe God as the creator who designs the universe with mathematical and aesthetic precision.</term> of the universe, the beauty of every created thing is the perfection of the work performed upon it by that Supreme Creator. Thus, in God, beauty exists before love; and being beautiful and lovable precedes being a lover.

...the proportionate, nor is every proportionate thing beautiful (as <note>original: "costoro" – referring to those philosophers who define beauty solely as proportion, such as the followers of Vitruvius</note> those thinkers have believed).

**SOPHIA:** What then is the beauty of corporeal things, which makes well-proportioned figures and bodies beautiful, if beauty is not proportion?

**PHILO:** Know that matter—the foundation of all inferior <note>The "inferior world" refers to the physical, earthly realm, which in Renaissance cosmology sits below the celestial and spiritual spheres.</note> bodies—is by itself formless and the mother of all deformity within them. However, when it is informed <term>informed: the philosophical concept where a "form" or spiritual essence is impressed upon raw matter to give it identity and shape</term> in all its parts through participation in the spiritual world, it makes itself beautiful. Thus, the forms radiated into matter from the Divine Intellect and the **World Soul**—or rather, from the spiritual and celestial world—are what remove its deformity and provide beauty. Consequently, beauty in this inferior world arrives from the spiritual and celestial world, just as ugliness and deformity are inherent to it because of its own formless and imperfect matter, from which all its bodies are constructed.

**SOPHIA:** Therefore every body would be equally beautiful, because they are all essentially informed by the superior world.

**PHILO:** I grant you that every body possesses some degree of beauty, which comes from the form that shapes its formless matter. But they are not equally beautiful, because these forms do not shape all inferior bodies in one perfectly equal way, nor do they remove the deformity of matter in the same manner in all of them. On the contrary, in some they remove only a small part of this deformity, while in others they remove more, and in increasing degrees. The more a form succeeds in removing material deformity, the more beautiful it renders the body; the less it removes, the less beautiful and more deformed the body remains. This difference exists not only among the various species of bodies in the inferior world, but also among distinct individuals.

<meta>This page continues the discourse between Philo and Sophia. He argues that the **Ideal notions** are not the essences and substances of things, but rather the productive and ordering causes of them. Whence he holds that **primary substances** are individuals <note>Aristotle's "first substance" is the specific, individual thing, like a particular man or a particular horse</note>, and that within each of them the essence of the **species** <note>species: the specific category or class of a thing</note> is preserved. And he does not want the Ideas to be primary substances (as **Plato** says), nor even secondary ones, but the primary causes of all corporeal substances and of all their essences composed of **matter** and **form**. Because its essence and substance is constituted of both matter and form, and since in the Ideas there is no matter or body, in them (according to him) there is neither essence nor substance; rather, they are the divine principle upon which all essences and substances depend—that is, the primary things as the first corporeal effects...

<meta>This page continues Philo’s explanation of the philosophical shift between Plato and Aristotle. On the previous page, Philo described how Plato prioritized spiritual "Ideas" over physical matter. Here, he explains Aristotle’s role as a "moderator" who brought philosophical focus back to the physical world to ensure that the study of nature (the "effects") could properly lead to an understanding of the divine (the "causes").</meta>

...[finding that] the **Philosophers**, through the doctrine of **Plato**, had become entirely removed from bodies, estimating that every **beauty**, **essence**, and **substance** existed only in the **Ideas**, and nothing in the corporeal world. Seeing that because of this they were becoming negligent in the **knowledge** of corporeal things—and in their acts, motions, and natural alterations, and in the causes of their generation and corruption—from which negligence there would result a defect and lack in the abstract knowledge of their spiritual principles; for a great knowledge of the effects ultimately induces a perfect knowledge of their causes. Therefore, it seemed to him time to temper the extreme in this, which perhaps in time would have exceeded the Platonic goal; and he demonstrated (as I have told you) that there are properly in the **corporeal world** essences and substances produced and caused by the Ideas, and that there are in it also true beauties, although dependent on the most pure and perfect Ideal ones. In Renaissance medicine, this refers to the proper mixing of qualities to maintain health.</note>.

**PHI.** Good and evil can exist within a single subject—not in the same respect, but in different ones. For a thing can be good in a small and apparent part of itself, but bad <note>original: "gattiua" (cattiva), meaning bad, wicked, or harmful</note> in its greater part, and more intimately and consistently. Such are the bad and **intemperate pleasures**: insofar as they delight, they are (and appear) good; but in themselves they are bad, because the good they derive from their form is united with the malice of the matter and submerged within it. Hence they are bad in themselves, even though they have some apparent good that delights. 

Furthermore, this is not an absolute good, nor is it apparent or delightful to everyone, but only to those **intemperate** desirers who are drawn toward the desire for their own minimal good without considering the excessive evil that lies beneath it. But those who are **temperate** are not deceived by that bit of apparent good, because they recognize the overwhelming evil with which it is mixed. Thus, they do not judge it to be delightful or desirable, but rather a true pain which ought to be abhorred, feared, and fled. Many such examples are found in the carnal appetite, for the majority of the pleasures of taste and of venereal touch, as well as other soft indulgences <note>original: "mollicie," referring to luxuries or physical comforts that weaken moral resolve</note>, are bad and pernicious.

**SO.** And are some of these carnal pleasures indeed truly good?

**PHI.** Yes: those that are temperate and necessary for human life and for the continuation of the species. Although these are carnal pleasures, they are (and are called) **honest** <note>The word "honest" here carries the classical sense of *honestas*, meaning morally honorable, virtuous, or proper.</note>, because they are measured and tempered by the **intellect**—the principle of honesty—and the desi- <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "deri," likely continuing as "desideri" (desires) on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo. ...or perhaps because they are neither beautiful nor deformed, and thus you neither desire nor abhor them. All other forms of <term>cognition<note>original: "cognitioni." Knowledge or mental apprehension.</note></term> regarding things that are good and beautiful are either of those things for which love or desire is their end—such as the cognition of food, which is followed by desire when there is a need for it—or they are of those things which are the end of desire, such as enjoying that food through union. Thus, desire and love are nothing other than a path from imperfect cognition leading toward perfect unitive cognition.

**PHILO**: Although love carries with it affliction and torment, anxiety and distress, and many other pains that would be long to recount, these are not its proper goal. Rather, its true end is the sweet delight which is the opposite of these. Nevertheless, you have spoken the truth—not regarding every love, but only regarding mine toward you. I see that its goal has never been pleasure nor delight; instead, its beginning, its middle, and its end are entirely made of pains, anguishes, and passions.

**SOPHIA**: How then does the rule fail in you? Why is your love deprived of that which every other love ought to achieve?

**PHILO**: This you may ask of yourself, and not of me. My part is to love you as much as my soul can contain; if you make that love sterile and deprived of its due end, it is you who must seek your excuse.

**SOPHIA**: I want you to seek your own excuse; for if your love is stripped of the proper goal you have assigned to love, it must be that yours is not true love, or else that delight is not love's true goal.

**PHILO**: The goal of all love is delight, and mine is the truest love. Its goal is to enjoy you with unitive delight <term>unitive delight: in Renaissance philosophy, this is the supreme pleasure found when two souls (and bodies) become one through love</term>, toward which the lover and his love are both directed. Nonetheless, not everyone who strives for a goal attains it—especially when the achievement of that goal must come from the hand of another. Such is the delight of the lover: it is the end toward which his love tends, but it will never come to pass unless the reciprocal love of his beloved leads him into it. Thus, that...

<summary>Sophia and Philo debate whether the true goal of love is delight or suffering; Philo argues that while love aims for "unitive delight," it results in pain if the beloved does not return the affection.</summary>
<keywords>Philo, Sophia, unitive delight, reciprocity, suffering in love, teleology of love, Neoplatonism</keywords>

For this reason, love for that person becomes so intense, burning, and effective that it captivates the senses, the imagination, and the entire mind, just as divine beauty would do when it draws the human soul toward itself in contemplation. ->**A B**<-
<note>The initials **A** and **B** stand for Antonio Blado (1490–1567), a master printer of the Italian Renaissance. Based in Rome, Blado was the official printer for the Papacy and the Roman people, known for his high-quality typography and prestigious commissions.</note>

This page features a central <term>woodcut</term><note>A relief printing technique where an image is carved into a block of wood; the raised surfaces are inked and pressed onto paper.</note> depicting a <term>crowned eagle</term><note>The eagle is a traditional symbol of power and imperial authority. Blado adopted this motif as his professional emblem to reflect the status of his press in the heart of Rome.</note> with its wings spread wide. 

The bird is framed within a shield-like border with jagged, decorative edges. Flanking the eagle's body are the letters **A** and **B**, identifying the printer. At the bottom of the image, the eagle’s talons are shown gripping a draped cloth or mantle. This <term>heraldic</term><note>Relating to the system of symbols and coats of arms used to identify families or institutions.</note> device served as a mark of authenticity, ensuring readers knew this volume was a genuine product of Blado’s esteemed workshop.
